15. Migration plan (proposal; each step mergeable, the system stays usable in between)
b: Status: agreed design, ready for implementation planning (2026-11-12). Source: design interview with the maintainer on the planning whiteboard. This file is the single source of truth for the orchestrator; where it contradicts older docs ( docs/daemon.md , docs/status-model.md , the former integration doc of the external orchestrator, docs/question-format.md ), this file wins and those docs are to be updated. Values marked (default) are configurable. Items marked (proposal) were not decided in detail by the maintainer and may be refined by the implementer; flag deviations in the PR description. 1. Goal and scope Gitoodo grows from a tray app into an open-source orchestrator that runs many Claude Code sessions deterministically across several machines, using a forge (Forgejo or GitHub) as the ledger. Open source, built for other people: all identifiers (labels, services, config keys, markers) are English and configurable. Human-facing text in the app follows the app language; what Gitoodo and its workers write on the forge follows the setting "Language on the forge" (app language, English, the issue's language or a fixed language; a repository can override it, #980). The existing integration of an external agent orchestrator is removed and replaced. It was only the reference for several mechanisms below (worktrees, usage limits, remote hosts). Clean start: no old German keywords or question format. Old German labels are written never and read only as their catalog role ( aliases.tsv , section 5.6). Version 1: classifier, dispatcher with local and remote workers, sweeper, gitoodo ask , answering questions in Gitoodo, orchestrator chat, Claude usage limits in the status bar, release planning (optional per repo). Later: screenshot-based hang detection (screenwatch), mobile app (QR pairing, LAN TLS), GitLab for the orchestrator (the existing GitLab adapter for the plain app stays), releasing dev to main from Gitoodo, AI review of PRs. 2. Principles 2.1 The system never blocks itself Reconstructible: every state can be rebuilt from facts on the forge after a restart, crash or lost cache. Local databases are caches, never the truth. Nothing waits forever: every waiting or locked state has a deadline or a way out and becomes visible to the human at the latest then. Fallback instead of standstill: when a service or path fails, the others keep working (e.g. polling instead of webhooks). Exception: a fallback must never hide a failure. Where it would, use self-start plus a clear error instead of a silent substitute (e.g. the app in orchestrator mode, section 4). Failures stay small: a problem affects one issue or one host, never the whole queue. Every component documents where it can block and how it heals (blockade tables below). The main host is not always on. When it is off, the system stands still; this is intended. After waking, every service first reconciles with the forge, then acts. 2.2 Facts and labels The forge is the only source of truth. Services write facts (comments, assignees, PRs, lease audit comments, question blocks) and labels. Each label group has exactly one owner – the component that makes that decision. Nobody else writes labels of that group. Owners recompute their group from the facts on every run and overwrite it; there is no "conflict resolution". Services are deterministic. LLMs run only inside workers and the chat. 3. Architecture 3.1 Components Name Binary / command Job Not responsible for Gitoodo (app) Gitoodo.app (binary renamed internally to gitoodo-app ) GUI, orchestrator chat, questions, status hosting services, writing service labels Classifier gitoodo classifier readiness, dependencies, PR links, answer detection, release planning starting workers, merging Dispatcher gitoodo dispatcher assigning issues, starting/stopping sessions, limits, hang detection, PR auto-merge classification labels, writing code Sweeper gitoodo sweeper removing merged branches and worktrees deleting unmerged work Ask gitoodo ask a worker's question to the human waiting for the answer Satellite gitoodo satellite hosts worker PTYs and the sweeper on a remote host scheduling MCP server gitoodo mcp the chat's tools file or shell access Attach gitoodo attach <issue> view/interact with a running session in any terminal – Worker a Claude Code session (no own binary) one issue, one worktree, PR labels, other workers, merging to main Forge adapter library in gitoodo-core uniform API for Forgejo and GitHub business logic Ledger Forgejo or GitHub (exactly one forge per project, configured per repo) issues, labels, PRs, milestones, branch protection running services One program gitoodo with subcommands; each service runs as its own process and system service, started and stopped independently. Today's gitoodo-cli becomes gitoodo . Shipping (#355): the direct-distribution app bundles the CLI as a Tauri sidecar ( bundle.externalBin , overlay src-tauri/tauri.sidecar.conf.json , built by scripts/build-sidecar.sh ). Installing copies it to a stable per-user folder ( paths::bin_dir , GITOODO_BIN_DIR overrides) and registers classifier and dispatcher there as system services with automatic restart (launchd KeepAlive , systemd Restart=always ; Windows: classifier only, task with restart on failure; the dispatcher needs named-pipe control first). The app shows app, installed CLI and running classifier versions and offers a reinstall on a mismatch. The sandboxed store builds ( store feature) ship no sidecar and install no services: they are a viewer and the orchestrator runs from the direct build or a manual CLI install. Today's daemon ( docs/daemon.md ) is split: queue/lease logic moves into the dispatcher, label hygiene into the classifier. Destructive catalog transfer on activation is dropped (section 5.6). Where things run: main host – classifier, dispatcher, sweeper, local workers, app. Satellites – gitoodo satellite (workers + sweeper), controlled by the main host's dispatcher over SSH. Forge adapters in v1: Forgejo and GitHub. Capabilities: issues, labels, comments, dependencies, branches, PRs, auto-merge, milestones, events/webhooks with polling fallback (default 5 min). 3.2 Communication App ↔ services: local socket / named pipe (as today's daemon: mode 0600, user-only pipe). Dispatcher ↔ satellite: SSH only (stdio bridge, JSON lines). No open ports on satellites. Workers never talk back to the dispatcher directly; they write to the forge ( gitoodo ask , PRs). Writes from the app (answers, approvals, chat actions) go straight to the forge; in orchestrator mode the app then nudges the classifier to re-read immediately. 4. The app Two modes , selectable in the app, with the consequences explained in the UI: Direct mode: the app polls the forges itself, as today. No orchestrator, no label maintenance; status is derived from assignees and PRs. Orchestrator mode: the app shows the services' picture via the local socket (classifier: issues/labels; dispatcher: workers, queue, leases, hosts), plus chat, worker control and limits. If the services are down, the app tries to start them; if that fails it shows a clear error state instead of data. It never silently falls back to direct mode. Repositories: connect a forge, Gitoodo lists all repos, the user switches them individually or in bulk. In the app a fetched repo is on (fully autonomous) or off ; pausing is an action on a repo that is on, not a level picked during setup (#599). Stored states: off (not fetched, disabled_repos ), observed (shown as "off": fetched, nobody writes; default for newly imported repos), paused (on and paused: classifier works, dispatcher assigns nothing), active (on). The stored values need no migration: observed reads as off, paused as on + paused, active as on. Switchable in the app and by chat (project focus, e.g. "only A and B now"). Since #569 the repository list selects all, by owner or row by row and switches the selection in one step; the repository's own settings (#926) edit the config-only options per repo (the human whose questions get assigned, whether release planning runs). Guided setup (#569): the onboarding offers orchestrator mode and hands over to the setup assistant (service, account and rights, labels, repo, local copy, skill and AGENTS.md , first worker; see setup.md ). The assistant writes only the marked Gitoodo section of AGENTS.md in the local copy, on request, and never commits. Issues from the app (#569): the orchestrator view creates an issue per repo, optionally with the ready label set at once. Questions: questions on which other issues wait are sorted first and show the number of waiting issues. After 2 h (default) unanswered – or the question's own deadline – Gitoodo notifies again. Status bar: per Claude login the remaining 5-hour and weekly limit with reset time; when locked, clearly when work resumes; stale values are marked as stale. Viewing sessions: live terminal view of any worker (local or remote) in the app. 5. Ledger: labels, questions, trust 5.1 Label catalog Names are canonical defaults; users can map them to their own names. Never created: type:* , needs-classification (nothing in the system consumes them) and answered (answers are detected from the comment order, section 5.4). Group (question) Label Owner Meaning Self-healing 1 Placement: where and how urgent? priority:p0 … p3 classifier, human dispatcher order. p0 now, p1 next, p2 normal, p3 some day missing → p2 os:windows / os:macos / os:linux classifier, human OS the worker must run on missing → any host; no matching host online → waits visibly, notify host:<name> human (optional) pins an issue to one host host offline long → notify 2 Readiness: may it start? needs-clarification classifier contradiction (dependencies, PR link); starts a clarification worker clarification fails → needs-human blocked classifier an open dependency lifted when all dependencies are closed; cycle → needs-clarification ready classifier may be worked on (see 5.3) unanswered approval blocks this issue and its dependents, visibly 3 Workflow: what is happening? in-progress dispatcher reserved, prevents double assignment, shows who works on it see 7.6 in-review dispatcher PR open, auto-merge to dev enabled, waiting for green CI CI red / conflict → new session; no movement → notify stalled dispatcher still failing after 3 restarts blocks this issue and its dependents, waits for the human 4 Human: is something waiting for you? needs-human question mechanism: whoever asks via gitoodo ask sets it; answer detection (classifier) removes it worker question, approval or clarification; the kind is in the question block deadline in the block, reminder (section 4) 5 Pull requests: is the PR clean? needs-issue-link classifier PR without issue; merge blocked by a failing status check lifted once the link is unambiguous 6 Release (optional) release:next human (also via chat) scope of the next release see section 10 7 Marker (no question) gitoodo classifier teal #29aea9 ; set on every open issue and open PR of paused and active repos, so you see the classifier handles it. Added only, never replaces another label; in no exclusive group missing → added; label missing → recreated Precedence: blocking wins ( blocked over ready ). Dispatcher candidates: open, ready , repo active , no in-progress / needs-human / stalled , all dependencies closed. 5.2 Manually set labels (not by the worker account) The forge records who set a label. ready by hand = approval; dependencies still win. blocked by hand without a dependency fact = deliberate hold until the human removes it; the classifier comments once. needs-clarification by hand starts a clarification worker. The chat may set the labels a human sets (priority, host: , release:next ), never service labels. 5.3 Trust and approval Issues and PRs by trusted authors (maintainers, own worker account, configurable list) become ready / are auto-merged without approval. Trusted from the start (#599): the connected account, the r

The app guides you through the orchestrator setup and does each step for you. On first start the onboarding offers orchestrator mode (preselected) next to the plain to-do list. With orchestrator mode, the onboarding sets up every repository picked in its repo step in one go, right after that step: you choose once what happens to issues that are already open and press Set up now . Gitoodo then installs the background service (the signed release reads tokens through the service helper without any keychain step; other builds grant the services access once, macOS may ask: choose Always Allow ), renames legacy labels and creates missing ones, switches each repo on, clones missing local copies into the clone folder, installs the skill for the worker agent and starts the dispatcher. Each part and each repository shows its own state; Try again repeats only what failed. Own label names, single repositories and agent instructions stay in the settings. First run (#337) The onboarding leads a first-time user from the account to a running worker: Repos to work on : every repository Gitoodo reads starts switched off. The step lists them unchecked, with search and "All"/"None"; only the checked ones are set up and switched on. A repository switched off here (or later in the settings) does not show in the sidebar. Setup : one confirmation sets up all checked repositories. Each shows its label preview (kept, renamed old → new , created) before anything is written, then its progress; Try again repeats only what failed. Legacy labels are read under their catalog meaning; nothing is deleted. The open-issue choice defaults to Check existing issues and ask : open contributions of other authors are never trusted on their own, the intake asks for an approval, which "Asked of me" answers per group or all at once. The merge style is preselected from what the repositories allow (Forgejo repositories that only allow fast-forward get fast-forward-only ). Workers : this machine is listed as a worker with its capacity (default 2, editable) and the agent found on it; machines named in host: labels that do not exist are listed with the issues waiting for them and can be made an alias of this machine. How it goes on : the live state (dispatcher, workers, ready issues), then either **Release an issue** (sets the ready label on an open issue of a switched-on repository) or **Create a test task** (a small issue that is ready at once), and where progress shows (board, sidebar, status). Switching a repository on records adopted_at . Every switched-on repository can be paused and switched on again where it shows: the play/pause button on its sidebar row (on hover and in the "…" menu) and in the board's repository header. Both write the same state as Settings → Repositories ( active / paused in orchestration.json ); pausing lets running workers finish. A short message confirms each switch. The emergency stop keeps its state across restarts: what ran when the app ended runs again, what was halted stays halted (a banner says so, with "Fortsetzen", which lets every repo continue in its own state). "Alles anhalten" in the title bar, in the tray menu, Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+H or gitoodo stop-all stops everything at once (see dispatcher.md , "Emergency stop"). Switching on more than three repositories at once asks first and names the count and how many workers run in parallel ( dispatch.max_workers , default 2). The sidebar picks several repositories at once: Shift-click picks a range, Cmd-click (macOS) or Ctrl-click (Windows, Linux) adds or drops one, Shift+arrow extends from the keyboard, Cmd/Ctrl+A picks every shown repository and Escape lets go. A bar at the foot of the list and the "…" menu then pause, switch on, star or move all picked repositories ("Pause 3 repos"). Groups nest: "New group inside" in a group's "…" menu, dragging a group onto the middle of another one, Alt+Right/Left (into the group above, out one level) or "Move to group …" (also M) put a group inside another, shown with the path ("Clients › Web"). A group never moves into itself or a group inside it. Each level is indented, keeps its folded state and counts what its subgroups hold. Groups can be picked like repositories; pausing or switching on a picked group acts on every repository inside it. Deleting a group moves what it holds up one level. The assistant below covers the same steps one by one, for a skipped onboarding step, later changes and single repositories. Open it from Settings → Setup assistant , or from Settings → Mode once orchestrator mode is selected. The assistant stores no progress of its own. Each time it opens, and whenever you press Check again , it checks the real state of the service, the accounts, the labels, the repository state and the dispatcher. It then continues at the first step that is still open. You can stop at any point and resume later, or run it again on a finished setup: steps that are already done stay done and are skipped. The assistant opens in its own window, shows one step per page with Back and Next and a progress bar of all steps, and moves on by itself once a step is done (#589). Everything the assistant does is also possible by hand. Each step below names the manual way. 0. Install Install the app from the download on the landing page (macOS DMG, Windows setup). On macOS, curl -fsSL https://gitoodo.com/install.sh | bash installs the app and the gitoodo command; on Windows, irm https://gitoodo.com/install.ps1 | iex does the same. Then open Settings → Setup assistant . The matching uninstall.sh / uninstall.ps1 removes the services and everything else again (see the README). 1. Background service Check: the classifier answers on its local socket and reports its version, its secret backend and whether its first poll has finished. Accounts the last poll could not read are shown as a hint. Assistant: registers the classifier with the system service manager and waits until it answers. This is launchd on macOS, a systemd user unit on Linux and a scheduled task on Windows. When the service is registered but silent, Set up service again restarts it. If the gitoodo command line program is missing (it is looked for next to the app, then on PATH ), the step says so. The assistant first copies the bundled CLI to a per-user folder and the services run that copy, so moving or updating the app does not break them; both services restart on their own after a crash or a reboot. The step shows the app and installed CLI versions; when they differ from each other or from the running classifier, Reinstall aligns them. Classifier and dispatcher each have Start, Stop and Remove. The store builds install no services. By hand: gitoodo service install|uninstall|start|stop [classifier|dispatcher|all] , gitoodo --version . On a system without a service manager, run gitoodo classifier in a terminal. gitoodo doctor checks the result. 2. Account and token Check: at least one account is connected and no account's token lacks a permission or has expired. Assistant: opens the account wizard. A token that needs renewing is replaced in the Replace token … dialog of that account. Tokens go to the system keychain only. By hand: Settings → Accounts. Orchestrator account (#764): per forge host the orchestrator acts as a chosen account. The onboarding step "Worker-Konto" recommends a separate worker account and guides through it per forge: create the account, give it write access to the repos (Forgejo/Gitea: collaborator with write or a team; GitHub: collaborator or team with Write; GitLab: Developer, Maintainer for protected branches), sign in as the worker account and create a token with the rights listed there (the orchestrator's rights without repository settings), and allow it to merge under branch protection. The token goes through the normal account wizard, so it lands in the system keychain only. The check then shows the worker account's login, missing scopes and every activated repo it cannot work in, with a link to grant access. Using the own account stays possible; the history then shows the user's name. Change and check it later under Settings → Accounts → Orchestrator-Konto. In orchestrator mode the onboarding step "Konto" says which account belongs there: the user's own account, with admin/owner rights for the setup; the worker account follows in the step "Worker-Konto". Automatic worker account (#764): where the own account may create accounts, the step "Worker-Konto" offers "Create worker account automatically" above the guide. Nothing is written before the user has seen a summary and confirmed it. Then four steps run in order, each with its state; a failed step is run again and continues where it stopped (every step is idempotent): Account. Forgejo/Gitea: needs a site administrator ( GET /user → is_admin ) and a token with write:admin . POST /admin/users with the chosen login and email, restricted: true (sees only what it is added to), must_change_password: false , full name "Gitoodo worker" as marker. GitLab self-managed: an administrator with the api scope (and Admin Mode, where it is on); POST /users with skip_confirmation , force_random_password , external: true , projects_limit: 0 , no group creation, and an admin note as marker. The login is checked (letters, digits, - , _ , . , at most 39 characters); the email defaults to a plus address of the own email ( alice+gitoodo@… ), Gitoodo never invents a domain. A login that already exists is used again only if it carries Gitoodo's marker; anyone else's account is never changed. Access. Per activated repo (or every listed repo when none is active yet) the worker becomes a collaborator with write (Forgejo/Gitea), or a member as Developer (GitLab; Maintainer only where a protected branch lets only Maintainers merge). Organisation repos get a per-repo collaborator as well, not a team: Gitoodo creates no teams and changes no organisation membership, so the worker only reaches the repos the user switched on. A failed repo fails the step with its reason; the retry skips what is already in place. Merge. Forgejo/Gitea: on protected branches with a merge allowlist the worker is added to merge_whitelist_usernames . GitLab: a protected branch where nobody may merge is listed for the user. Anything that cannot be done is listed under "Still for you" with the repo. Token. Forgejo/Gitea: the token endpoint only accepts basic auth (Sudo does not apply), so Gitoodo sets a random one-time password as admin, creates the token gitoodo-<time> with exactly the worker scopes ( read:user , write:repository , write:issue ) by basic auth and immediately sets another random password nobody knows. GitLab: POST /users/:id/personal_access_tokens with api and an expiry of 364 days. The token is stored through the normal account path (system keychain only, rights recorded, service access granted) and chosen as the host's worker account; the check below then runs as usual. The step leads with that card ("Create the worker account automatically") wherever it is possible; the manual guide sits behind "Set it up myself instead", the reasons behind a collapsed "Why a worker account?". A line under the step title says which way applies ("Gitoodo creates the worker account for you" or the guide). Admin without admin scope. Where the own account is a site administrator but its token lacks the admin scope, the card stays and asks to confirm admin rights once: Forgejo/Gitea: the user enters the own password (and, if the forge asks, the code of the authenticator app). The core creates a short-lived token with basic auth ( POST /api/v1/users/{login}/tokens , scopes write:admin , write:repository , write:user ; the one-time code goes out as X-Forgejo-OTP and X-Gitea-OTP ), runs the setup with it and deletes it right after ( DELETE /api/v1/users/{login}/tokens/{id} ), also when the setup fails. If that delete fails (a one-time code may have expired), the step names the token so the user can delete it under Settings › Applica

gitoodo dispatcher runs in the foreground (own process, own service later) and starts one worker (Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI, see "Worker launch per agent") per ready issue, each in its own git worktree behind a PTY. It is a client of the classifier: it reads the read model, claims work with next , reports with done and never writes labels itself. stalled and needs-human go out as Request::Flag ; only the classifier sets them. What it does Push loop (5 s): repos in an active state, ready issues by score, host choice ( choose_host , local host only for now), claim via the classifier, lease, worktree ( dispatch.worktree_root , branch dispatch.branch_prefix ), worker start. Limits come from dispatch.max_workers (default 2, so a first setup does not start workers in many repos at once), cores_per_worker , each machine's own "workers at once" (#967, see "Workers per machine") and min_free_memory_mb . The slots are shared fairly across repositories (see "Fair share across repositories"). Readiness: an issue without the ready label (or a legacy alias such as status:bereit ) is only ready by a trusted author and a complete body, and never in a repo whose backlog setting is New for issues from before adoption (intake reason backlog ; it waits for approval). Every new ready decision logs classifier.ready with via = label or trusted_author (issues ready when first seen at debug); classifier.ready_seen counts those per poll, split into label and trusted_author . One instance (release-gate review M7): at start the dispatcher takes an OS file lock ( dispatcher.lock ) in its config folder and in its state folder, before it touches any lease; the OS frees it when the process dies, so a crash leaves no stale lock. A second dispatcher for the same folders (second install, a restart while the old one still runs) exits at once, or under a service manager waits until the lock is free. Only then, and after it owns the control socket, does it release leases. Leases (60 s): every running worker's lease is renewed. Each local lease names its owner (machine, process id, start time). At start only the local leases whose owner is provably gone are released: an earlier process on this machine that no longer runs, or a lease from a version that did not record owners. Leases owned on another machine and satellite leases are never deleted at start; they expire by time or follow the unreachable grace. The forge-side gitoodo:lease v1 comments are never deleted. An issue whose dead local lease is released at start goes back into the queue ( Flag::Release on the next push tick: in-progress removed, ready set), so a killed dispatcher leaves no orphans behind (#337). Orphans (#337): an issue labelled in-progress without a running worker is orphaned (no lease, lease expired, worker ended, or a local lease of unknown origin). It takes no worker slot. The dispatcher cleans orphans up by itself (#868): once a minute it looks for them in the repos it may write to (paused or active), and one that is still orphaned after orphans::GRACE_SECS (five minutes) goes back to ready through the classifier ( Flag::Requeue , the same fresh read and swap as "Reset"); a worker that starts meanwhile, here or on a satellite, ends the grace. Logged as dispatch.orphan_requeued . The board lists orphans apart on the workers page until then; "Reset" ( reset_orphans , core orchestration::orphans::reset ) does it at once: it reads each picked issue fresh, leaves any the dispatcher runs a worker for, and swaps in-progress for ready . The classifier marks the leases this machine's dispatcher took ( LeaseHolder.ours , Lease.origin names the machine), so "runs on another machine" is shown only for a known other machine. **Broken orchestration.json (M9):** the dispatcher keeps running. Running workers stay managed with the last valid configuration (lease renewal, merges, restarts, hygiene, remote polls); no new worker or automation starts until the file is valid again (wait reason config_invalid ). The problem is reported once per distinct problem: the log ( dispatch.config_invalid ), a desktop alert ( config_invalid ) and config_problem in the status, each with the file path and for a parse error the line and column, never the file's content. gitoodo doctor prints the same check. A valid file clears it ( dispatch.config_valid ). Broken from the start, there is no fallback and nothing is dispatched. Hang policy: no output and no hook ping for dispatch.hang_timeout_seconds restarts the worker in the same worktree; after dispatch.max_restarts restarts the issue is flagged stalled . A locked login (see "Usage limits") is waiting, never a hang or a restart. Machine faults (#982): a start that fails before the agent runs is the machine's fault, not the issue's: the agent is missing or signed out, or the clone, the worktree or the spawn fails (here or on a satellite, also on a restart). See "Machine faults" below. Exit with a pull request: merge_when_ready (the forge's auto-merge where the forge itself requires checks, else merge pinned to the head SHA once the checks pass). Pending pulls are retried every minute; failed checks restart the worker. Exit without a pull request counts as a restart. After a dispatcher restart (#565) the waiting pulls are rebuilt from the forge: an open pull on the dispatcher's own branch for the issue ( <branch_prefix>/<n>-… , the pull's branch name as the forge reports it, even when the issue's title changed) whose issue is open, has a worktree here and does not wait for a person ( needs-human , stalled ). A person's own pull that closes the same issue from another branch is never taken up, updated or merged. Merge gate ( dispatch::merge::decide , pure): the style is the configured one (default squash) when the repo settings allow it, otherwise the first allowed of squash, fast-forward-only, merge, rebase. Every merge is pinned to the checked head SHA (Forgejo head_commit_id ). The style per repo is the one set in that repository's settings → Merging ( repos[].merge_method , #926), else the global dispatch.merge_method ; the first attempt of each pull logs the effective style and why ( merge style squash (repo setting) , squash (dispatcher default) , or squash (dispatcher default rebase is not allowed by the forge) ). Behind-base update (#383): a pull whose branch is behind its base is brought up to date locally and the checks are awaited again. Fast-forward-only and rebase rebase the branch onto the base (linear history); squash and merge commit merge the base into the branch. The push uses the credential-free askpass path of the worker push; the branch is pushed only with --force-with-lease on the pull's head SHA, so a foreign push is never overwritten. The worker's worktree is used while it has the branch checked out clean at that SHA; when it is gone (cleaned up, a restart) or holds other commits (a later run that never pushed) or uncommitted changes, the update runs in a temporary detached worktree of the repository's clone, from the head the forge reported, with hooks off, and the worker's worktree stays as it is. A real conflict is not retried: the pull gets a comment naming the files and the issue is stalled with the cause conflict . At most 3 updates per pull (a base that still moves on: base_moving ); a failed update does not count as one, is tried once more, and a second failure in a row stalls the issue with update_failed and the reason in the log ( dispatch.branch_stuck ). A satellite run is updated on the satellite (#391): the dispatcher sends update_branch over SSH and the satellite runs the same update with its own git credentials (helper or SSH key, no token, no extra forge permission), pushing with the same lease. When the satellite has no usable credential or is unreachable, the run log states why and the issue is stalled with update_failed . The forge's own "update branch" call is not used, except on GitLab projects with fast-forward or semi-linear merges: there GitLab rebases the branch itself (its rebase call on the merge request) and the new head is awaited like a push; a branch GitLab cannot rebase (conflict) takes the local update. GitLab's 406 ("branch cannot be merged") is a refusal like 405/409, so a refused, stale branch is updated instead of failing. Which checks gate: the checks the forge requires, read from the classic branch protection and, on GitHub, the rulesets of the base branch ( GET /repos/{o}/{r}/rules/branches/{branch} , rule required_status_checks ); on Gitea/Forgejo the protection rule named like the base branch, else the first glob rule that matches it ( release/* , {main,dev} ; by priority where reported), whose required contexts may be globs too; on GitLab the head pipeline when "Pipelines must succeed" is on (pending until it exists; a pipeline of an older head counts as pending). Only then is the forge's auto-merge used, since without required checks it would merge at once. When the forge requires nothing or hides its rules, every check the head reported gates (statuses and check runs: success, neutral and skipped pass, pending waits, a failure fails), plus the repo's extra checks. A head with no check at all waits dispatch.ci_grace_seconds (default 180 s, 0-3600) from when the gate first saw it, so CI that has not started yet is not taken for "no CI"; a repo without CI merges after that. Failed merge calls: the next attempt waits 1, 2, 4 … up to 30 minutes (a back-off round does not use up a merge attempt), and the alert merge_failed names a cause category ( auth 401/403, protection , conflict or behind, not_acceptable 406, server , other ), never the forge's text; the same cause for the same pull is alerted once, then again only after 1 h, 2 h … up to a day; a new cause at once. The full error stays in the dispatcher log. A merge the branch protection refuses ( protection ) is diagnosed (#942): the dispatcher reads the rule of the base branch (repository account first, merge account second) and names the cause ( merge_allowlist , check_missing , check_failing , approvals , outdated , unknown , unreadable ). An outdated branch is updated and merged again, a failed required check goes back to the worker. Every other cause is kept in merge-blocks.json in the state folder, one entry per pull request, notified once per pull request and cause (the entry survives a restart, so a restart does not notify again) and shown as a card in "Asked of me". For the merge allowlist, a required check that never reports and missing approvals the dispatcher stops merging; it reads the rule again every 120 s, and at once after "Allow the merge account" on the card, and merges once the cause is gone. These waits use up no merge attempt. GitLab rules are not read ( unreadable ). The same causes are checked ahead of time when a repository is added or its autopilot switched on (the setup check: readiness items merge-account , worker-push , reporting-checks , approvals ); the check only shows them and never holds the switch up. See Branch rules that work with the autopilot . Sweeper (5 min and after each merge): removes worktrees of merged or closed issues and their local branches; a worktree with unmerged commits is reported once ( needs-human ) and kept. The same tick runs the reconcile round of the repo hygiene (#771): Gitoodo's worktrees and branches without lease or worker, also after a crash, in every checkout and on satellites; stale remote branches; maintenance; and the disk guard before each new local worker. Shutdown: SIGTERM or ctrl-c stops the workers, removes the control socket and exits. Logs go to dispatcher.jsonl in the log folder ( logging ) with issue keys only, never tokens; stderr only takes bootstrap output ( dispatcher.stderr.log ). Agent programs (#963). Every supported coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI) is found by itself; nothing has to be set. Only when an agent is not found does the dispatcher settings page offer that agent's own program path ( dispa

t: Branch rules that work with the autopilot
b: The autopilot merges a finished pull request with the merge account : the worker account of the repository, or the repository's own account when no worker account is set up. A rule on the base branch can refuse that merge. When it does, Gitoodo reads the rule, names the cause and acts on it (#942): Cause What Gitoodo does The branch is behind its base Updates the branch the way the merge style needs and merges again. A required check failed Sends the pull request back to its worker. The merge account may not merge Shows a card in "Asked of me" with Allow the merge account . A required check never reports Shows a card naming the check, with the link to the setting. Approvals are missing Shows a card with the count (given of required), with the link. The rule cannot be read, or says no more Shows a card with the link to the branch settings. Each cause is notified once per pull request. While a setting refuses the merge, Gitoodo makes no merge attempt; it reads the rule again every two minutes, and at once after **Allow the merge account**. When the cause is gone, the merge runs and the card disappears. Reading a branch rule needs admin rights on most forges. Gitoodo reads it with the repository's own account first and the merge account second; when neither may read it, the card says so. The setup check When you add a repository or switch its autopilot on, Gitoodo reads the rule of the base branch right away and compares it with what the autopilot needs (#942). Switching on is never held up: the autopilot is on at once, and the check runs in the background. When something would stop the autopilot, a notice appears in the corner of the window with one plain sentence per problem and the same actions as the card: Allow the merge account where Gitoodo can change it, otherwise Open the setting , and the link to this guide. The same items stay in the repository's readiness checklist until the rule fits. Item Checked Action Merge account The merge account is on the rule's merge list (Forgejo/Gitea merge whitelist, GitHub push restrictions). Allow the merge account (admin rights needed), or link. Merge account may push The merge account has at least write access to the repository. Link to the collaborator or access settings. Required checks report Every required check was reported on the newest open pull request whose checks have all finished. Without such a pull request, or without named required checks, the item is left out. Link to the rule. Approvals The rule requires no approvals. Required approvals are flagged because the autopilot then waits for a person on every pull request. Link to the rule. The configured merge style is checked by the existing item Merge style of the checklist. Nothing alarming is shown for what Gitoodo cannot know: a rule the token may not read, a forge that does not report it, an account whose login is unknown, or a repository without an open pull request leaves the matching item out. GitLab is skipped for now (see below). What the rule should allow Merging by the merge account. If the rule lists who may merge (or push), the merge account must be on that list. Required checks that report. Every required check must be a check the pipeline of the repository actually reports, with exactly that name. A check that was renamed or removed from the pipeline blocks every merge. Approvals the autopilot can get. Required approvals hold every pull request until a person approves it. Keep them only if a person reviews each change; Gitoodo does not approve its own work. "Behind the base" is fine. Gitoodo updates the branch by itself, so a rule that refuses outdated branches works. Forgejo and Gitea Settings → Branches → the rule of the base branch ( /settings/branches/edit?rule_name=<rule> ): Enable merge whitelist : when on, add the merge account under the allowed users ( merge_whitelist_usernames ). Allow the merge account does exactly this; it needs admin rights on the repository. Enable status check : the listed contexts ( status_check_contexts , globs allowed) must match checks the pipeline reports on pull requests. Required approvals ( required_approvals ): only official, current approvals count. Block merge on outdated branch ( block_on_outdated_branch ): fine; Gitoodo updates the branch. Merges by the merge account need the write right on the repository. GitHub Settings → Branches → the protection rule of the base branch: Restrict who can push to matching branches : the merge account must be listed (users or teams). Allow the merge account adds the user; a team has to be changed by hand. Require status checks to pass : the required checks must be reported on pull requests. Require branches to be up to date is fine. Require approvals : the count of approving reviews. GitLab Settings → Repository → Protected branches: the merge account needs Allowed to merge on the base branch, and the project settings decide whether pipelines must succeed. Gitoodo does not read these rules on GitLab yet: the setup check skips them, and when a merge is refused there, the card links to the setting.

h: Deleting a repository on the forge
b: Gitoodo orchestrates coding agents as workers. A worker reads forge text (the issue, its comments) and runs code on the machine. This page says whose text may steer a worker, how a worker runs, and how the forge token stays out of the worker's reach. It answers the release-gate review findings H1 (untrusted forge text steering an unattended worker) and H2 (token-carrying git calls in worker-writable folders). Who is trusted A login is trusted for a repository when any of these holds ( intake::Intake::is_trusted , one rule for intake, answers, briefs and worker context): it is trusted automatically (#337, #916, acting::auto_trusted ): the token owner of the connected forge account, the worker account Gitoodo writes as, and every login Gitoodo wrote as before on that forge (earlier worker accounts, kept in orchestrator_writers ). All are derived at runtime from the accounts set up in onboarding and the write history, never copied into trusted_authors (so no migration is needed), and follow a token renewal or an account switch; Settings → Dispatcher shows them as "Automatically trusted" (own account, worker account, earlier worker account) and they cannot be removed there. Other bots, Ghost (a deleted account) and agent accounts are not trusted automatically; it is the repository's configured human ( human ); it is listed in Settings → Dispatcher → Trusted authors ( trusted_authors ); an entry that opened no issue or pull request and wrote no comment in any configured repository for 90 days is marked "not active" there with a remove button (#943). The check reads at most 20 repositories and 4 pages per listing, is cached for 6 hours and marks nobody when it cannot read everything (for example on GitLab, which has no repository-wide comment listing); an entry is never removed automatically. An approval card of an untrusted author offers "Trust this author" (#916), never for system or bot accounts: the app adds the login to this list through its settings write path (the dispatcher never writes orchestration.json ), the author's open approvals leave the card and their issues turn ready on the next pass, and "Undo" takes only this login back for ten seconds; the forge reports write, maintain or admin permission on the repository, or membership in the organisation that owns it. A failed lookup counts as untrusted. Everyone else is untrusted, including anyone who can comment on a public repository. What reaches a worker Issue: only issues of trusted authors (or approved by a trusted person, spec 5.3) become ready and are dispatched. Title and body of a dispatched issue reach the worker. Comments, start brief ( orchestration::brief::worker_brief ) **and gitoodo worker context **: only trusted people's comments appear as discussion, Gitoodo questions or answers. A comment of an untrusted person is never labelled "Answer" or "question", whatever markers it carries. Depending on the repo's worker mode (below) it is left out with a count (unattended) or quoted in a fence that its own backticks cannot close, under a heading that marks it as untrusted data (guarded; untrusted quotes have their own, smaller size budget, so they cannot push a trusted answer out). When trust cannot be judged (forge unreachable), every comment is left out. Answers ( hygiene::reconcile_issue ): only cards and answers posted by trusted people count. A stranger cannot post a card that names themselves and then answer it, and a stranger's answer marker or plain reply to a card without a header login does not release the issue. The intake's own approval and clarification rules ( intake::scan ) were already trust-checked; the issue author may still answer the intake's clarification. Automations: only events of trusted actors start an automation session, and the prompt carries kind, number, author and link, never bodies. The title of an issue opened by an untrusted person is left out even when a trusted person's comment on it is the event. The orchestrator chat ( gitoodo mcp for a human-led chat session) still shows all comments: a person reads along and confirms forge and configuration changes on proposal cards. The chat can also relay an explicitly requested human instruction directly to a running worker. The system prompt treats issue bodies, comments and tool results as data, never authorization to send. The MCP server enforces the chat scope and instruction bounds; the dispatcher protects unsent human input. This relay relies on the chat model to recognize the human request and its intended recipients, and does not independently verify the request against the conversation. Worker mode per repository Settings → Repositories → (repo) → "Workers with permission checks" sets worker_permissions in orchestration.json : Mode Agent flags Untrusted comments unattended (default) Claude Code --dangerously-skip-permissions ; Codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox , worktree trusted; Gemini --yolo left out guarded Claude Code --permission-mode auto --add-dir <clone git dir> ; Codex --sandbox workspace-write --ask-for-approval never with network access and the clone's git directory as an extra writable root, worktree untrusted; Gemini --yolo --sandbox --include-directories <clone git dir> quoted as untrusted data unattended stays the default because workers must finish without anyone answering prompts, and it is safe for the trust boundary above: only trusted text reaches it. guarded adds the agent's own checks as a second line, for repositories where more is at stake, typically public ones. Automation sessions always run unattended; their prompts carry only trusted text. Satellites get the same mode; the clone's git directory is only added on the main host. Codex workers run Codex's interactive terminal UI (#934). Their folder trust is a setting of the session only ( -c projects={…} ), never written to the user's Codex config: unattended trusts the worktree like a Claude Code worker (the repository's own Codex settings and hooks load), guarded records it as untrusted, so nothing from the repository configures Codex and the sandbox flags stay as set. Gitoodo's hooks ( gitoodo hook stop|activity ) are passed per session too and run with --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust , so no hook review waits in the terminal. Hook events of the user's own config.toml are emptied for the session ( -c hooks.<Event>=[] , "What a worker loads" in docs/orchestrator/dispatcher.md ); hooks Codex reads from elsewhere (a hooks.json , the repository's own settings in a trusted worktree) still run without their review. -a never means a guarded worker never waits for an approval: Codex's sandbox refuses what it does not allow and the model gets the refusal. What a worker loads Workers start lean: without the user's MCP servers, plugins, skills, slash commands, memory and extra tools, but with the repository's instructions, Gitoodo's hooks and the permission mode above (details and flags: docs/orchestrator/dispatcher.md , "What a worker loads"). Besides the tokens, this keeps a worker that reads untrusted text from reaching the user's personal connectors (mail, calendars, other accounts). A repository can allow named MCP servers ("MCP servers for workers", worker_mcp_servers , none by default); everything a server can reach is then within a worker's reach too. Settings that come with the user's agent configuration itself (login helper, provider environment, deny rules, and for Claude Code the user's own hooks) still apply. Sub-agents and nested agent sessions (#952) Settings → Repositories → (repo) → "Workers may use sub-agents" sets worker_sub_agents in orchestration.json (off by default). A worker is one agent session; off keeps it that way, so its work, its usage and its permission mode stay in the session the user can see: Agent Off (default) On Claude Code --disallowed-tools Agent : the sub-agent tool (older name Task ) is denied for the session the agent's own choice Codex -c features.multi_agent=false -c features.multi_agent_v2=false : the multi-agent features (names from codex features list ) are off the user's features Gemini CLI no command-line switch exists (its agents are a settings-file feature); only the brief and the process check below apply unchanged Both switches are settings of that session only; nothing is written to the agent's own configuration. In both modes the start brief tells the worker never to start another coding agent session or agent command-line program from its shell, and the dispatcher (a satellite for its own workers) looks at each issue worker's process tree every 15 seconds: a claude , codex or gemini below the worker's own agent process (its own helper processes of the same agent excepted) is logged as dispatch.nested_agent (issue, run, agent, process id, never the command line), and with the setting off it is ended ( SIGTERM ; Windows taskkill /T ). The check lists processes with ps (Windows: Get-CimInstance Win32_Process ); where that fails, the round is skipped. Satellites of older versions only get the flags. Residual risk: the check finds the three agents by program name, every 15 seconds; a renamed binary or a session shorter than that is not caught, and other agent programs are not known by name. The flags and the brief are the first line; the check catches what slips through. Automation sessions belong to no repository; they keep the agent's own features and are not checked. Public repositories On a public repository anyone can open issues and comment. Untrusted issues wait for a trusted person's approval and are never dispatched on their own. Untrusted comments never steer a worker in either mode. What remains is the code and data in the repository itself (a trusted person merged it) and whatever a worker fetches from the internet while it works; for that second line, use guarded . Worker follow-up issues A worker may propose a follow-up issue ( gitoodo worker follow-up , spec 8.3); the dispatcher's broker creates it with the connected account's token. The worker's text is treated as untrusted data, although the worker account is its author: Mediated: the proposal needs the worker's capability, a live lease of that worker on its issue and the repo setting worker_follow_ups (on by default; switch it off where workers should never write to the issue tracker). The worker gets no token and no forge client. Bounded: one-line title up to 200 characters, body up to 16 KiB, at most dispatch.max_follow_ups_per_run per run (default 3) and 10 per repository and hour; a title that matches an open issue refuses the proposal. Chains stop at depth 3: a follow-up of a follow-up of a follow-up may not propose another one ( follow_up::MAX_DEPTH , the depth is in the marker). Refusals name only fixed reasons, never forge errors. Approval is opt-in: the issue carries the gitoodo:follow-up marker in the footer Gitoodo appends; <!-- in the worker's text is defused, so it cannot forge that or any other Gitoodo marker. By default the intake makes a follow-up the worker account opened ready like the account's own issues, so another worker may pick up its body without a human reading it first; the bounds above are what limits a worker that runs wild. A repository's human who wants to read every proposal first switches on "Approve each follow-up before it is worked on" (repository settings → Workers, stored as follow_up_approval in its orchestration.json entry; the default for repositories without their own choice is dispatch.follow_up_approval , Settings → Dispatcher). Then the intake asks for approval like for an issue from outside (a "no" closes it), the read model never counts it ready without the ready label, and with the intake rule for outside issues switched off such follow-ups wait untouched. Switching approval off again releases the follow-ups still waiting, as if approved. A marker in an issue by anyone else always counts as an outside contribution. h: Install and upgrade: gitoodo host install <name>
Version check and other systems in the app (#441)
Windows machines and the remote shell (#958)
b: A satellite is another machine that runs workers for the main host's dispatcher (spec 7.9). Network and SSH live only in crates/core ; no port is opened. Forge credentials stay on the main host; assistant subscriptions are provisioned separately as described below. Pieces gitoodo satellite : persistent service on satellite.sock (0600) holding worker PTYs; on Windows on the named pipe \\.\pipe\gitoodo-satellite-<user> that only this user may open. gitoodo satellite --stdio is a pipe to it (it starts the service when missing, on Windows detached from the SSH session), so workers survive SSH drops. The bridge ends when its stdin closes, the SSH session hangs up (SIGHUP), the service closes the connection, or nothing moved either way for 15 minutes; a subscription sends a sign of life every minute so it never idles out. Bridges of gone sessions used to stay forever (#965). Protocol: JSON lines, the same cmd / reply / frame vocabulary as the dispatcher socket ( dispatcher_rpc.rs ), plus hello , spawn , kill , subscribe , ask , ask_done , copy_state , copy_receive . A bridge session runs requests in a row; subscribe and attach turn it into a stream. Bridge: system ssh -o BatchMode=yes ... -- <target> gitoodo satellite --stdio ( GITOODO_SSH replaces the program, used by tests); on Windows .local\bin\gitoodo.exe satellite --stdio , relative to the home folder the SSH session starts in. gitoodo host add <name> <ssh-target> : detects the remote shell, connects, compares versions, saves {name, ssh, shell, platform} only. platform ( macos , windows , linux ) is the system the machine reported; the app saves it too when it adds, installs, checks or probes a machine and the system differs from the stored one. A machine set up before the system was stored gets it in the background: 30 seconds after the app starts it checks each machine without one, and again every 10 minutes while one is still unknown (offline). The dispatcher starts every machine with it, so an issue for that system waits as offline while the machine is away, not as no_platform . A version mismatch is a clear error with the check command ( ssh <target> gitoodo --version ). The handshake also compares builds, see "Build identity" below. Dispatcher: polls every host (20 s), offers satellites as host candidates, starts workers with spawn (the satellite creates the worktree in its own clone). Unreachable host: no new work, leases wait for the grace and are then released ( lease_action ). Own copies (#965): a satellite keeps its clones under ~/gitoodo/repos/<owner>/<repo> in its own home; the main host never sends one of its own paths. spawn 's prepare carries the repository's credential-free forge address ( origin ). The main host makes and updates the copy itself before each spawn ( satellite_copy.rs ), so the machine needs no forge access and no network permission for its own git: it fetches the base (and the worker branch, when the forge has it) with the connected account into its own copy, filling in whatever a partial copy lacks, asks the satellite what it holds ( copy_state : tracking refs, partial or not) and sends a git bundle of the rest ( copy_receive : a header with refs, size and SHA-256, then base64 chunks of 512 KiB; at most 4 GiB). The first copy gets the full history, later starts only what is new (the satellite's heads are the bundle's prerequisites); a copy left partial by an older build gets the full history once and then stops being partial, so no lazy fetch is ever needed there. The satellite checks size and checksum, unbundles, moves origin/<base> (and origin/<branch> , or drops it when the forge no longer has the branch), sets origin to the forge address and starts the worktree from it ( prepare.synced ); a restarted worker so gets its pushed branch back. The forge's branch wins over what an earlier run left on the machine: a local branch behind it is fast-forwarded, one apart from it (the branch was updated onto the base, or someone pushed) is set to it, and commits of its own the forge lacks stay under refs/gitoodo/kept/<branch>/<sha> (log satellite.branch_kept ); a kept worktree that is clean and only behind is fast-forwarded, one with uncommitted work or own commits stays as it is. The token stays on the main host: it is in no bundle, frame, error or log. Satellite paths (#965): the main host sends none of its own paths. The worker's cwd is ~/gitoodo/worktrees/<repo>/<number> (or below a ~ -relative worktree root), the hygiene requests name the satellite's own roots, a configured absolute agent path that does not exist there falls back to the agent's name, and the hook and status-line commands in --settings (Claude Code) and in -c hooks.* (Codex) carry a placeholder the satellite replaces with its own gitoodo , quoted as one shell word. Delivery when the forge moved on: the main host fetches the forge's worker branch into the delivery's scratch repository; a bundle that lacks its commits is never pushed (no force). The main host sends them to the satellite's copy as origin/<branch> , and the worker gets a reason that says to rebase or merge origin/<branch> and deliver again. A satellite whose build lacks copy_state is the machine fault outdated (see below) and gets no start; any other failure of the transfer falls back to the machine's own git clone, and its reason is added to the checkout: error. Branch updates (#383) on a satellite go the same way: the main host sends the base first, update_branch with via_host rebases or merges offline and answers with a bundle of the new head, which the main host pushes with the account ( --force-with-lease on the old head). Worker PATH (#965): a satellite service started by ssh or launchd has a short PATH ; its workers get the agent's folder, the service's PATH , the login shell's folders and the known install folders that exist ( ~/.local/bin , ~/.cargo/bin , Homebrew, ...), so the agent and the tools it calls are found as in a terminal. Failed remote starts are sorted by who answered (#965): a satellite that answered with a reason was reached, its fault is the reason's class ( agent_missing , agent_login , no_checkout , start_failed , outdated ); only no answer at all is unreachable . Each class pauses new workers on that machine once (one notice per machine, not per issue) and names the machine, the agent, the repository and one action there ("update Gitoodo there" for an outdated build); "restart the service" is offered only for this computer. An unreachable machine gives no notice: nobody can fix it from here, it is retried by itself, the work goes to the other machines, and Settings → Worker machines shows it offline. gitoodo attach [<host>] <issue> : raw terminal, detach with Ctrl-], the worker keeps running. Questions: gitoodo ask on a satellite ( GITOODO_SATELLITE=1 ) asks the service, which forwards it on the main host's subscription; the main host posts and confirms, then the worker is parked. Hooks: gitoodo hook stop|stop-failure|status-line|activity on a satellite ( GITOODO_SATELLITE=1 ) sends hook to the service instead of a dispatcher socket (see "Hook events" below). Remote worker lifecycle The satellite records workers that end on their own and measures output silence. The main host polls with report (exits are drained, so each is delivered once) and applies the same hang policy as for local workers: silence for the timeout restarts the worker (a spawn without prepare , in the worktree that already exists there), after the maximum it is stalled . report also carries the satellite's own subscription usage. The satellite starts reading it (keychain, usage endpoint, codex app-server ) with the first report , not at service start, so a satellite no main host talks to stays idle and small (#769). A login that no longer works is reported apart from a reached limit (#994): the agent's usage.problem is not_signed_in and no old values stand for it. The satellite says so only on the agent's own word: Codex's account/rateLimits/read answers with an auth error, or Codex says so in a notification or on its stderr while the query fails ("could not be refreshed", "sign in again", a rejected refresh token, HTTP 401, "authentication required"); Claude's usage endpoint refuses a token that has not expired yet (401/403). A query that only times out or fails otherwise stays unknown. Such a login typically still passes codex login status ("Logged in") after its refresh token was revoked. The main host then waits with login_expired ("the agent's login there no longer works; sign in again on that machine") instead of usage_gate for that agent there; with the worker pool it names this reason over a usage limit of the other agent, because only a person ends it. After signing in again the next query (at most five minutes later) clears it. A worker that exits on its own is handled like a local one (finish/merge flow). A worker killed by the main host leaves no exit record. Hook events A satellite has no dispatcher, so a worker's gitoodo hook <event> there talks to the satellite service ( satellite.sock , on Windows its named pipe) with the dispatcher's hook request ( issue , event , usage ). The service holds the worker's terminal, knows its delivery and reads its own agent login, so it applies the event itself, exactly as the dispatcher does for a local worker ( crates/cli/src/satellite_turns.rs ; locally Hub::hook and Hub::check ): Every hook is a sign of life: report.silent counts from the later of the last output and the last hook, which the main host's hang policy reads. stop without a result (no pull request yet) is looked at after the same 30 s grace: a worker at its usage limit is left to its reset; one a person typed into lately (attached from the main host) is marked idle ; the others get the reminder once and end at the next such turn end ( satellite.worker_nudged , satellite.worker_idle ). activity and stop-failure cancel a pending look. stop after the pull request ( gitoodo worker pr confirmed by the main host) ends the worker (Claude Code, Codex; satellite.worker_finished ), and its exit record says code 0 , so the main host merges at once as for a local worker. A Codex stop asks this machine's Codex limits again (at most every 30 s). stop-failure marks the worker limited and locks this machine's Claude login ( Tracker::limit_reached ); status-line brings the status line's usage windows. Both go into the next usage round, so they show in report.providers ; the lock outlives the next usage query until a report shows room or its end passes. At the end the worker gets continue ( satellite.worker_continued ). list carries the satellite's idle , limited and limited_until (this machine's lock end). The main host shows them on the worker's tile and does not take a limited worker's silence for a hang ( login_locked ), as for a local worker. The main host's own usage figures stay its own: a satellite's status line describes the satellite's login. Robustness: the state lives on the satellite, so nothing is lost while the main host is away; it reads the result with its next list and report . The hook waits at most 3 s for the service and never fails or prints; no service, a busy one or an older one that refuses hook ( bad request or "does not handle") is silent, as a missing dispatcher is locally. An older satellite sends nothing and lists no states, so the main host behaves as before; an older main host ignores the states. The events carry an issue key, the event's name and usage percentages, never a token or a path. A run the main host tracks is not released as vanished for 45 s after start, so a slow poll cannot drop a fresh worker. Unreachable satellites keep the lease grace rules above. Run state of remote workers lives in memory only; after a dispatcher restart the lease table and the satellite's worker list decide (listed: renewed, not listed: released). Updating the main host's app or dispatcher does not touch a satellite's workers: they run on the satell

Gitoodo cleans up its own worktrees, branches and temp files: after merges, after crashes and resets, after an uninstall, and above all in the user's own checkouts, which serve as clones since #755. Code: crates/core/src/hygiene/ (decisions, the only removing code), the dispatcher's crates/cli/src/dispatcher_hygiene.rs and the satellite's crates/cli/src/satellite_hygiene.rs . Safety rule In a user checkout Gitoodo only ever runs git worktree remove on worktrees below the worktree root that are its own, git worktree prune , git branch -D <prefix>/<number>… and a fetch of the base. User branches, stashes, the index and working-tree changes of the checkout are never touched ( crates/core/tests/hygiene.rs checks this). Anything that holds work that would be lost (uncommitted files, commits on no remote branch and not in the base by content) is never removed silently; it is reported as a leftover. Ownership Every worktree Gitoodo creates (dispatcher and satellite) gets the marker file gitoodo-owner (JSON: issue key, branch, time, host) in its git folder ( <checkout>/.git/worktrees/<name>/ ), so the working tree stays clean. Its branch is <branch_prefix>/<number>-<title> (default prefix gitoodo ). Older worktrees without a marker count as Gitoodo's when they lie below the worktree root on such a branch. Agent sessions ( agent-session/* ) never match. Reconcile round At dispatcher start (after the leases of the earlier run are released) and every sweep interval (5 min), the dispatcher scans the checkouts of the configured repos, every checkout a folder below worktree_root points to, and the orphan folders there. Before deciding it fetches the base. State Action lease held or worker running (here or on a satellite) keep a "Solve with an agent" session of the issue (#919) keep merged (content in the base, also after squash), clean remove worktree and local branch issue closed, nothing unsaved remove worktree and local branch issue open, clean and pushed (abandoned) remove worktree, keep branch for a new start waiting for a human ( needs-human , stalled ) or unknown keep unsaved work report as leftover folder deleted by hand worktree prune , branch as above orphan folder (no worktree any more) report as leftover A "Solve with an agent" session ( docs/agent-session.md ) works in the issue's worktree without a lease; its record in own-sessions/ keeps the worktree in use until the person closes the tile or hands the issue back. The lease sweep and the cleanup after a merge also delete the local branch once its work is merged or its issue closed. A lease taken between scan and removal wins (checked again right before). Satellites take part on the main host's word: hygiene_scan returns their items, the main host decides with its leases and the forge, hygiene_apply carries the decisions out; a running worker's worktree is refused there too. A backup of a satellite's leftover (#886) runs through hygiene_bundle : the satellite commits the unsaved files and sends the branch beyond the base branch as a git bundle, the main host pushes it as the backup branch with the account's token (satellites hold none) and only then orders the removal. On its own, 30 s after start and every 5 minutes, a satellite sweeps old temp files (also inside the shared sessions folder) and removes what is merged in content (the scope the main host sent last, kept in satellite-hygiene.json ). Leftovers Reported items go to hygiene.json in the state folder ( HygieneStatus ): cleanup state, leftovers with host, issue, branch, commits and uncommitted files, disk reading and errors. The board ("All repos") lists the leftovers, each with: Discard: removes the worktree and branch with whatever they hold. Push as backup branch and remove: commits uncommitted files, pushes the branch as <prefix>-backup/<rest>-<time> with the account's token, then removes it. On a satellite the main host pushes from the satellite's bundle (#886). The app queues the decision in hygiene-requests.json ; the dispatcher handles it within 5 s and runs a round. dispatch.leftover_expiry_days (default 0 = off) discards leftovers automatically after that many days. gitoodo diagnose lists the leftovers. Saved by itself (#873, #886): the user does not have to decide. A leftover on this host or on a reachable satellite that can be backed up and was first reported an hour ago ( AUTO_BACKUP_SECS ) is pushed as a backup branch and removed in the next round, exactly like "Push as backup branch and remove" ( dispatch.cleanup_auto_backup ). The newest 20 saves are kept in hygiene.json ( saved : issue, branch, time); they need nobody, so no page lists them (#924). A failed push stays a leftover and is tried again next round; a worktree a worker uses is never touched, and nothing is pushed while Gitoodo is halted. Orphan folders without a branch still wait for a decision; a satellite that is offline is saved once it is back. Discarding is never automatic unless the expiry is set. Remote branches Hourly, for every configured repo with the sweep rule on, remote <prefix>/* branches without an open pull/merge request, without a lease and without a local branch are deleted once the issue is known (open or closed) and the newer of last commit and first sighting is older than dispatch.remote_branch_grace_hours (default 24, 0 = off). At most 10 per round, one per second, through the forge adapters (Forgejo/Gitea, GitHub, GitLab; every deletion in the forge audit log and the dispatcher log). Disk guard (#771, #970) Code: crates/core/src/hygiene/disk.rs (levels, readings), crates/cli/src/dispatcher_hygiene.rs ( disk_tick ), crates/cli/src/satellite_hygiene.rs ( watch_disk ), crates/cli/src/freeze.rs (pausing a worker's processes). Every 15 seconds the dispatcher (and every satellite for its own machine) reads the free space of the volume holding worktree_root and, when it differs, of the volume holding Gitoodo's own data (state, logs; the agents' data sits next to it). The free-space reading is cheap ( statvfs , or GetDiskFreeSpaceExW on Windows); sizes of folders are never measured in this loop. Level Begins below Ends at or above Effect low the smaller of dispatch.min_free_disk_mb (default 10240 MiB) and dispatch.min_free_disk_percent (default 5 %) the limit plus a margin no new worker starts on that machine critical the smaller of 2 GiB and 1 % of the volume, never above the low limit the limit plus a margin the machine's running workers are paused as well The margin is a fifth of the limit, at least 1 GiB and at most the limit itself, so a reading that wobbles around a limit does not flap: with the defaults on a big disk the warning begins below 10 GiB and ends at 12 GiB, the pause begins below 2 GiB and ends at 3 GiB. 0 switches the low limit off (and with it critical ). A volume without a reading (a missing drive, an error) counts as fine and never holds work back. The worst volume sets the machine's level. Low : no new local worker starts (satellites still take work; with none online the dispatch wait reason is disk_low ), DispatcherStatus.disk_low is set and a reconcile round runs. Critical : the running local workers are paused, not stopped: on macOS and Linux their whole process tree gets SIGSTOP (resumed bottom-up with SIGCONT ), on Windows every thread of the tree is suspended ( SuspendThread / ResumeThread ). A paused worker is never counted as hung and its silence starts afresh when it resumes; one that ends during the pause leaves normally, and stopping a paused worker resumes it first so it can exit. They resume on their own once the level drops back to low or ok . Satellites run the same loop for their own disk, refuse a new worker at critical ("the disk of this machine is almost full; free up space there") and report their level in the status reply. The main dispatcher places no new worker on a satellite whose disk is low or worse and lists it in DispatcherStatus.disk_hosts . DispatcherStatus.disk carries the machine's level, every volume (path, roles, free and total bytes, both limits, the bytes to free so the level ends) and the number of paused workers. The app shows a warning in the status bar while a disk is low or worse (this computer first, then worker machines by name) and posts one system notification; it posts again only when the warning gets worse ( low → critical ) or after the disk was fine in between. Every text says how much to free and how: on this computer "Remove build output" under Settings → Storage, on a worker machine freeing space there. The status bar entry and the notification open Settings → Storage. What fills the disk After each reconcile round, at most every 15 minutes (at once when a warning begins and after "Remove build output"), the dispatcher measures on a background thread what lies on the worktree volume and stores it in storage.json ( disk ): Gitoodo's worktrees (kept leftovers counted apart), their build output (the folders "Remove build output" would remove now, so only worktrees without a running worker), the agents' data of Gitoodo's runs and Gitoodo's own data (each only when on the same volume), everything else as "other programs", and the free space. The parts add up to the volume's size. Settings → Storage shows them as one bar with a row per part and, during a warning, the warning with a button "Remove build output (size)". Stalled by machine faults (#982) An issue that is stalled only because its machine could not start a worker (no run reached the coding agent) is not the user's to fix. At dispatcher start and after a paused machine started a worker again, such issues in repositories the dispatcher may write to go back to ready , each with a short note marked <!-- gitoodo:auto --> . Which issues qualify is kept in start-faults.json in the state folder, filled the first time from the dispatcher's run log. Issues stalled for any other reason (hangs, failed checks, a stalled worker) are left alone. Details in dispatcher . Agent data (#971) Coding agents keep data per session or per working folder in their own home folder. Gitoodo removes the part that belongs to its own runs once their worktree is gone, and only that part. Code: crates/core/src/agent/cleanup/ (one module per agent; tests with fake homes in cleanup/tests.rs ). Whose data. An entry is Gitoodo's only when the working folder the agent recorded is a Gitoodo worktree: exactly <worktree_root>/<repo>/<number> , compared component by component (case-insensitive on Windows, no .. ), and either the agent also recorded the issue branch <branch_prefix>/<number>… of that worktree or Gitoodo recorded the worktree itself ( agent-worktrees.json in the state folder, written when a worktree is created and on every sweep for every worktree with the gitoodo-owner marker). Folder names are never matched by prefix. The user's own sessions in the repository's checkout, in session-* folders below the root or anywhere else never match. Agent Removed per run Proof Claude Code ( ~/.claude , or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR ) projects/<encoded folder>/ , and for each of its sessions file-history/<id>/ , session-env/<id>/ , todos/<id>-*.json , debug/<id>.txt The folder name is the encoded worktree path (every character other than A–Z, a–z, 0–9 becomes - ). Because that encoding is ambiguous, every transcript in it must also name the same worktree as cwd , and none may name another branch than the worktree's issue branch; a folder whose transcripts lack this stays. Paths longer than 200 characters (the agent shortens those) are never matched. Codex ( ~/.codex , or CODEX_HOME ) sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*-<id>.jsonl , archived_sessions/… , shell_snapshots/<id>.* The first line ( session_meta ) names the worktree as cwd and, without a ledger entry, its issue branch ( git.branch ). Gemini CLI ( ~/.gemini , or GEMINI_CLI_HOME ) tmp/<sha256 of the folder>/ , history/<sha256 of the folder>/ Only worktrees in Gitoodo's ledger; the folder name must be the hash of the exact worktree path.
